quote: The Bank would receive payment messages instructing transfers on the core ledger in anonymised form and would not know the identity of the payer and payee.
actor: CB (Bank of England as core-ledger operator)
transaction_scope: standard online mode (platform model, pass-through wallets)
modality: unconditional for routine operation; extraordinary access runs via PIPs (see F9)
justification: The joint BoE–HMT proposal says the Bank receives payment messages in anonymised form and would not know payer or payee identity. This is a statement of inability to know, not only that the Bank will not use the data. PIPs anonymise personal data before any sharing with the Bank (doc 3 p. 16, p. 74). The consultation response turns this into a commitment backed by intended legislation (doc 4 p. 28). The 2026 update reports technical and structural safeguards in the architecture (doc 17 p. 7). No routine identity key held by the Bank is documented, so the value is no rather than yes.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 28: The Bank commits to exploring technological options that would prevent the Bank from accessing any personal data through the Bank’s core infrastructure.

quote: The alias design allows privacy for the payer from the payee and vice versa, but not privacy from their PIPs.
actor: PSP (Payment Interface Provider); payer's and payee's own PIP
justification: The Bank's technical paper states explicitly that a user's own wallet provider knows who they are even when a disposable alias is used. The privacy design protects users from counterparties, not from their PIP. The joint CP gives PIPs the identity records and says personal data is anonymised only before sharing with the Bank, which implies PIP-side linkage (doc 3 p. 16, p. 57). The point-of-sale PoC shows transaction data viewable by payer and payee PIPs (doc 6 p. 22, tested). The value rests on an explicit statement, not on the KYC-plus-intermediation inference barred by §6.5.
counter_evidence: doc 2 p. 21: PIP and ESIP access to transaction data within the CBDC system should be limited to the legal and regulatory minima

quote: any law enforcement or Government agency that seeks to access and process digital pound users’ personal data from PIPs would have to do so on a lawful basis in compliance with the Data Protection Act 2018.
actor: law enforcement agencies, competent authorities, Government agencies
modality: lawful basis under DPA 2018 (s.31 law-enforcement purpose; formal request or court order; UK GDPR Art 6(1)); suspicious-transaction reporting by PIPs
justification: The PIP is named as the holder from which authorities obtain personal data, so the route is via_PSP and not n/d. The consultation response confirms that law enforcement engages with PIPs 'and not directly with the Bank' (doc 4 p. 29). The 2020 paper adds suspicious-transaction reporting by PIPs (doc 1 p. 32). No route via the CB is documented.

quote: Our current thinking is that this functionality would not be available at launch, but we will continue to explore device offline payments and review this position.
transaction_scope: offline (deferred offline proposed; device offline excluded at launch)
justification: No offline mode is an adopted commitment. The design note proposes only deferred offline payments, in which funds remain on the ledger and settle once a party reconnects (doc 16 p. 4). Those payments therefore pass through the ordinary PIP-linked flow, so they are not private. Device offline, the only potentially private mode, is excluded at launch under current thinking. Experiments that tested device offline do not establish adoption (doc 12 p. 14: no final decision). Because the status is option, this is not a commitment.
counter_evidence: doc 12 p. 11: Devices did not store a transaction record, and payments were effectively anonymous

quote: Just like opening a bank or other payment account, some level of identity verification would be required when opening a digital pound wallet, in order to prevent financial crime.
limits: basic tier: limited-ID, low-value payments; no amount stated
justification: Every wallet requires some level of identity verification, and the same wording is repeated in the response (doc 4 p. 28). The tiered wallets that are envisaged accept 'limited ID' (doc 3 p. 77). That is KYC-lite that still verifies identity, so it does not count as a no-identity route. The value is explicit; the §6.6a inference is not needed.
counter_evidence: doc 3 p. 77: users might be able to open a basic digital pound wallet with limited ID

quote: To establish and maintain these relationships, PIPs would require identity information of wallet account holders, which would allow them to carry out KYC checks and comply with AML regulations.
justification: PIPs require identity information and run KYC checks for wallet holders. The response confirms that PIPs would be required to identify users (doc 4 p. 28). The design note on intermediaries lists KYC at onboarding among PIP duties (doc 14 p. 7).

quote: In addition to law enforcement to fight crime (operating via law enforcement agencies engaging with PIPs under rules already approved by Parliament and not directly with the Bank), these are likely to be limited to:
actor: law enforcement agencies via PIPs; authorities for PIP failure and payment-dispute resolution
modality: conditional: lawful basis (DPA 2018); PIP failure management; unresolved disputes (Financial Ombudsman-type); data framework to be presented to Parliament
justification: The response names the extraordinary circumstances in which personal data held by PIPs becomes relevant to authorities. These are law enforcement, PIP failure and dispute resolution, governed by a data framework to be approved by Parliament (doc 4 p. 28). This prevents F1 = no from being read as absolute. The list beyond law enforcement is hedged as 'likely'.

quote: Programmable money would be both prohibited through primary legislation and technically impossible in the architecture.
justification: The authorities ruled out government- or central bank-initiated programmable functions (doc 3 p. 83) and committed to a legislative guarantee (doc 4 p. 31). Programmability is limited to PIP features that require user consent. Holding limits are a cap on balances, not purpose, expiry or blocking restrictions.
counter_evidence: doc 3 p. 82: so long as they are lawful, observe any restrictions (for example, maximum user holdings

quote: To promote innovation, choice, and efficiency in domestic payments as our lifestyles and economy become ever more digital.
justification: Efficiency in domestic payments is part of a declared primary motivation. The motivation is reaffirmed in later documents (doc 4 p. 19; doc 11 p. 5).

quote: There are other motivations for developing the digital pound. These include supporting financial inclusion and improving domestic payments resilience and cross-border payments
justification: Financial inclusion is declared as a secondary, non-primary motivation. It is repeated in Box D (doc 3 p. 40) and in the assessment themes (doc 9 p. 16).
counter_evidence: doc 3 p. 90: these benefits are unlikely to present themselves in the same way in the UK

quote: To sustain access to UK central bank money – ensuring its role as an anchor for confidence and safety in our monetary system, and to underpin monetary and financial stability and sovereignty
justification: Sovereignty and monetary-anchor stability are named in the first primary motivation, with further detail in Annex 1 (doc 3 p. 106). The flag rests on sovereignty. Monetary-policy transmission is explicitly not a motivation (doc 3 p. 52).
counter_evidence: doc 3 p. 52: Remunerating the digital pound, either positively or negatively, to make monetary policy more effective is not a motivation

quote: The digital pound could support the uniformity of money by replicating the role of cash in a highly digitalised economy.
justification: Sustaining retail access to central bank money as cash declines is the core of the first primary motivation (doc 3 p. 28). Payments resilience is a further declared motivation (doc 3 p. 40).

quote: Like current digital payments, the digital pound would not be anonymous because the ability to identify and verify users is needed to prevent financial crime.
justification: Financial-crime prevention appears only as a design requirement that justifies non-anonymity, not as a declared objective. Under the contract, a requirement to comply with AML rules does not set this flag, so it stays 0 (not documented as an objective).

quote: We are determined that the UK should remain at the forefront of innovation in money, payments and financial services.
justification: Innovation and competition in payments form a primary motivation (doc 3 p. 28, p. 36). The 2024 response also frames the project around competitiveness (doc 4 p. 18).

quote: We consider there are two primary motivations:
justification: Two primary motivations are declared jointly and said to 'go hand in hand', with no single one ranked first. They are repeated in doc 4 p. 19 and doc 11 p. 5.

value: cash_substitute_resilience + monetary_sovereignty_transmission (sustain access to central bank money / singleness); payment_modernisation + innovation_competitiveness (innovation, choice, efficiency)
quote: These two motivations go hand in hand.
justification: The two primary motivations are listed on the same page: (1) sustaining access to central bank money, which underpins stability and sovereignty, and (2) innovation, choice and efficiency in payments. Each maps onto two flags. Later documents phrase the first as 'singleness of money' (doc 11 p. 5).

quote: We are continuing our evaluations of various ledger technologies and architectures, including relational databases, NoSQL and distributed ledger technologies
modality: platform: centrally governed distributed database preferred in TWP (option); Lab demonstration ledger centralised with Hyperledger Cacti bridge to a smart-contract platform (tested)
justification: The technical paper leans towards centrally governed distributed databases but keeps a range of approaches under assessment (doc 2 p. 52; doc 5 p. 18). The CP calls the platform model technology-agnostic (doc 3 p. 57). The 2025 update confirms evaluations of ledger technologies are ongoing. Lab and prototype-ledger work are tests, not choices (doc 17 p. 5; doc 18 p. 9).
counter_evidence: doc 2 p. 52: the use of centrally governed, distributed database technologies, might be a more efficient and appropriate approach than the use of DLT solutions
